lesson.text: Quick memory: last unit, angles. How many degrees is a right angle? 90°: a square corner.
A point is an exact place. A line goes on for ever both ways. A ray starts at a point and goes on for ever one way. A line segment has two end points.
Parallel lines never meet, like the rails of a train track. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle.
Angles can be acute (less than 90°), right (90°) or obtuse (between 90° and 180°). Triangles are named by their angles too: a right-angled triangle has one right angle.
Shapes are sorted by their sides and angles. A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides. A rectangle has four right angles.
A line of symmetry folds a shape so that both halves match exactly. A square has 4 lines of symmetry.
Try it in the world: build a shape with one line of symmetry in your world, like a house front. Check it with a friend standing on the middle line. Next: tables, line graphs and pie charts.

exercises.prompt: How many sides does a hexagon have?
A square has four right angles.
exercises.explain: Every corner of a square is a right angle.

exercises.prompt: What is a line that starts at a point and goes on for ever one way called?
exercises.explain: A ray has one end point and goes on for ever the other way.

exercises.prompt: A triangle can have two right angles.
exercises.explain: Two right angles make 180°, which leaves nothing for the third corner.

exercises.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
exercises.hint: Fold it long-ways and short-ways. Do the corners match on a diagonal?
exercises.explain: It folds in half along the middle both ways: 2 lines.

exercises.prompt: Which capital letter has a line of symmetry?
exercises.hint: Imagine a mirror down the middle of each letter.
exercises.explain: A has a line of symmetry straight down its middle.

exercises.hint: What makes a rectangle? Does a square have it?
exercises.explain: A rectangle has four right angles. A square does too, with all its sides equal as well.

exercises.prompt: Parallel lines meet if you make them long enough.
exercises.explain: Parallel lines stay the same distance apart for ever, so they never meet.

exercises.prompt: Finish the build so both halves match, like in a mirror.
exercises.hint: Each block needs a twin the same distance from the red line on the other side.
exercises.explain: Every block has its twin on the other side of the line.

exercises.hint: Less than 90° is acute; exactly 90° is right; between 90° and 180° is obtuse.
exercises.explain: 30° and 75° are acute, 90° is right, and 120° and 150° are obtuse.

exercises.prompt: Sort them by their lines of symmetry: none, one, or more than one?
exercises.hint: Imagine folding each one so the halves match. How many folds work?
exercises.explain: None: F and G. One: A and an isosceles triangle. More than one: a rectangle (2) and a square (4).

exercises.prompt: Sort the shapes by their pairs of parallel sides.
exercises.hint: Look for sides that run the same way and never meet.
exercises.explain: No parallel sides: a triangle and a kite. One pair: a trapezium. Two pairs: a rectangle and a square.
